Embroidered cloths made by the Paracas culture on the desert south coast of Peru, between about 800 and 100 BCE, and counted among the finest textiles of the ancient world. They survive because the dry desert of the Paracas peninsula preserved what was buried there.

Most come from large cemeteries such as Wari Kayan, where the dead were seated, then wrapped in many layers of cloth into large mummy bundles. Some mantles took years of work. Weavers used cotton and dyed camelid wool in many colours, and embroidered rows of figures: animals, masked flying beings and people holding staffs or heads. The Paracas also practised skull shaping and skull surgery.

The Paracas tradition fed into the Nazca culture that followed on the same coast, which kept the textile skill and also made the Nazca Lines. Andean peoples, including later the Inca, valued fine cloth above gold, and Andean textiles stayed a main form of wealth and art.
